```{r load}
# data from data-raw/vignette_method.R, the methodology article's bundle
vd <- function(f) system.file("vignette-data", f, package = "knowledge", mustWork = TRUE)
x <- readRDS(vd("method.rds"))
reg <- x$settings
pk <- x$picks
sc <- as.data.frame(x$scope)
val <- function(key) gsub(";", ", ", reg$value[reg$key == key], fixed = TRUE)
n0 <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
issue <- function(n) sprintf("[#%s](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/knowledge/issues/%s)", n, n)
species <- c(BT = "bull trout", CH = "chinook", CO = "coho", GR = "grayling", ST = "steelhead",
             WCT = "westslope cutthroat trout")
key_words <- function(k) {
  paste(species[[sub("_.*$", "", k)]], if (grepl("_rear$", k)) "rearing" else "spawning")
}
words_and <- function(v) if (length(v) < 2) v else paste(paste(v[-length(v)], collapse = ", "), "and", v[length(v)])
sc$share <- sc$groups_both / sc$groups
sc$margin <- sc$null_heldout_curve - sc$dev_curve
under_half <- sc$key[sc$share < 0.5]
withheld <- sc$key[sc$grade_withheld]
# a key whose curve failed has no margin and no grade, and the run's flag for it reads FALSE
curved <- sc[!is.na(sc$margin), ]
closest <- curved[which.min(abs(curved$margin)), ]
# from data-raw/vignette_cut_points.R, the stream-splits article's bundle
cp <- readRDS(vd("cut_points.rds"))
pr <- as.data.frame(cp$premise)
cp_lim <- function(s) {
  v <- cp$setups$grad_max[cp$setups$setup == s]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  v
}
at_site <- function(net, status) {
  v <- pr$at_site_pct[pr$network == net & pr$catch_status == status]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  v
}
pct <- function(v) if (v >= 10) sprintf("%.0f %%", v) else sprintf("%.1f %%", v)
lim_pct <- function(s) paste0(signif(100 * cp_lim(s), 3), " %")
gs_ch <- x$gradient_sensitivity$pick[x$gradient_sensitivity$key == "CH_rear"]
ch <- sc[sc$key == "CH_rear", ]
# the prior's figures: a step of 2.5 on the cloglog scale, and the share of each prior beyond three scales
prior_sd <- as.numeric(val("prior_sd"))
p_norm <- 2 * stats::pnorm(-3)
p_cauchy <- 2 * stats::pcauchy(-3)
# the words on the cuts: on the published network a site with fish starts its own segment far more often than an empty
# one, less often than on the earlier build, and about as often as an empty one on the minimal network; chinook
# rearing's slope limit is steeper on the published network than on the minimal one, and the parent setup agrees with
# the minimal one. The bundle's full-network pick is this article's own, so a promotion that moves chinook rearing stops
# the build here until data-raw/vignette_cut_points.R is rerun
stopifnot(nrow(pr) == 6, at_site("published_145", "fish") > 3 * at_site("published_145", "zero"),
          at_site("published_92", "fish") > at_site("published_145", "fish"),
          abs(at_site("minimal", "fish") - at_site("minimal", "zero")) < 1,
          cp_lim("published") > cp_lim("minimal"), cp_lim("parent") == cp_lim("minimal"),
          # "its build is a slightly earlier link"
          package_version(pr$link[pr$network == "minimal"][1]) < package_version(pr$link[pr$network == "published_145"][1]),
          length(gs_ch) == 1, identical(gs_ch, cp$setups$pick[cp$setups$setup == "published"]),
          # the groups: chinook rearing's split is quoted, and in every key the never-caught groups outnumber the
          # all-caught ones
          nrow(ch) == 1, identical(ch$groups_both + ch$groups_all + ch$groups_none, ch$groups),
          all(sc$groups_none > sc$groups_all), ch$groups_all >= 1,
          prior_sd == 2.5, round(exp(prior_sd)) == 12)
# the words: the table holds every published key (the bundle's gradient limits come from data/thresholds.csv); every
# published key drops some groups, and more than half for the keys named; the publishing test withholds some
# keys and publishes others, and its closest call is decided by less than one unit of deviance. A bundle without
# `scope` would make every comparison logical(0), which stopifnot() passes
stopifnot(nrow(sc) > 0, setequal(sc$key, x$site_gradient$limits$key), all(sc$groups_both < sc$groups),
          length(under_half) >= 2,
          length(withheld) >= 1, any(!is.na(sc$margin) & !sc$grade_withheld), nrow(closest) == 1,
          abs(closest$margin) < 1, abs(closest$margin) >= 0.05,
          # the caption's sign: at zero or above withheld, below published (away from a tie the summary's rounding
          # could blur)
          with(curved[abs(curved$margin) > 1e-3, ], identical(grade_withheld, margin <= 0)),
          # the settings the prose quotes
          identical(val("prior_sd"), "2.5"), identical(val("se_region"), "1"), identical(val("folds"), "5"))
```


The tuning chooses the thresholds of a fish habitat definition, the few limits on a stream's size and slope that say
where a species spawns or rears, from the Province's fish sampling records, and grades each stream by how often the
species is caught on streams like it. Two textbooks set out how such a choice is made well: *Statistical Rethinking*
[@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking] and *Bayesian Data Analysis* [@gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata]. This article reads
the tuning against them: what it does as they teach, where it departs and why, and what we test next. It is a record
of where the method stands and where it is heading; the [methodology article](tuning-method.html) sets out its steps.

**The answer.** The tuning judges habitat definitions the way *Statistical Rethinking* teaches: on watershed groups
left out of the fit, telling two apart by the uncertainty of their difference, and keeping the near-ties together
rather than naming one winner. Its three main departures are each defensible for a habitat definition whose job is to
rank streams. The score measures how well a habitat definition ranks streams within a watershed group, not how often
the species turns up in a new one; the prior (an assumption about a value made before seeing the data) is used as a
penalty that finds one best value, not a full posterior (the spread of values the data and prior together allow); and
the thresholds are reported as one choice and a range, not a distribution. Three things should change: a check on how
the choice is made does not fully hold its test data out, the two models the publishing test compares treat a site
from an unfamiliar data set or period differently, and the stream slopes the habitat definitions read depend on where
fish were caught. The terms are gathered in a [glossary](#terms) at the end.

## What does the tuning do? {#tuning}

For each species and life stage, the tuning builds a grid of habitat definitions around those of
[`link`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/link/) [@link], the R package that maps habitat on BC's streams: a
floor on stream size, a ceiling on slope, and for some an exception for small streams near a large river. Each habitat
definition sorts every site crews electrofished into habitat or not.

The **scorer** is a regression of whether the species was caught at a site on that sorting. Beside it sit the area
fished (the effort) and two **sampling terms**, the data set the record comes from and its period, which are
differences in how crews sampled that a habitat definition must not be credited for. Each watershed group the scorer
keeps (the Province divides its streams into these large drainages) also gets its own **base rate**: how often the
species is caught there, other things equal. The **score** is the scorer's deviance at sites in watershed groups left
out when the habitat definition, effort and sampling terms were fitted, a measure of how badly it predicts the catch,
summed over sites; lower is better. (Each left-out group's base rate is then fitted on its own sites, as the next
sections explain.)

The groups are dealt into `r val("folds")` **folds**, and each fold in turn is left out of the fit and scored. Habitat
definitions whose scores lie within one standard error of their difference from the best are **close calls**, and
among them we choose the one that changes `link`'s current habitat definition least. Then a second model, the **curve**, a smooth surface of how often the
species is caught against stream size, distance to a river and slope, gives every stream the species can reach that
has a size and a slope a **grade**. The **publishing test** publishes those grades only if the curve scores better on
the left-out folds than no habitat definition at all.

## The checks, at a glance {#glance}

Each row is one question the books raise, what the tuning does, and where that leaves it. The sections below take
them in turn.

```{r glance}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  question = c(
    "Is the score taken on data the fit did not see?",
    "Are two scores told apart by the uncertainty of their difference?",
    "Does the score predict a new watershed group?",
    "How wide is a close call, and which close call is chosen?",
    "Does the check on the choosing hold its test data out?",
    "Is the prior a regularising prior at Bayesian Data Analysis's default scale?",
    "Does the prior give a posterior?",
    "Are thresholds reported as a distribution?",
    "Are watershed groups pooled?",
    "Which watershed group does the grade describe?",
    "Is the publishing test a fair comparison?",
    "Is an unfamiliar data set or period read the same on both sides of the publishing test?",
    "Is the catch rate per square metre the same however much area is fished?",
    "Is a miss an absence?",
    "Are the inputs measured?",
    "Is a stream's slope independent of the catch?"),
  `what the tuning does` = c(
    "Whole watershed groups are left out of each fit and scored",
    "Yes: the standard error of each difference, over watershed groups",
    "No: each left-out group's base rate is refitted first",
    "One standard error; the close call nearest link's current habitat definition",
    "Not fully: the scores it chooses from were fitted with its test groups in",

    "No: it is fitted as a penalty, which finds one best value",

    "Fixed in the scorer, with groups of one outcome dropped; pooled in the curve",
    "An average group",

              "departs", "should change", "departs, defensibly", "departs", "departs", "should change"),

## Is the score an honest test? {#score}

A model judged on the data it was fitted to always looks better than it is: the honest test is data it has not seen.
When the data come in clusters, *Statistical Rethinking* separates two tests:

> "If we wish to validate a model against the specific clusters used to fit the model, that is one thing. But if we instead wish to compute predictions for new clusters, other than the ones observed in the sample, that is quite another." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 426]

The tuning leaves out whole watershed groups, the strict form, so no site in a scored group helped estimate how much
the habitat definition, the effort or the sampling terms matter. But before a left-out group is scored, the scorer
refits that group's base rate on that group's own sites. So the score asks whether the habitat definition puts the
catches on the right streams within a group, not how many catches a new group would hold. Every habitat definition
gets the same refit, one fitted value per group, so by our reasoning (not measured) each is flattered by about the
same amount: the comparison between habitat definitions holds, while the score itself is not a prediction for a new
group. That is the right question for a habitat definition that ranks streams, since how common a species is in a
watershed is not the habitat definition's to predict. The score is also taken at one best estimate, where the books
average it over the posterior [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 210; @gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata, p. 174].

## How are two habitat definitions told apart? {#se}

Two scores are close or far by the uncertainty of their difference, not of each score alone:

> "we don’t use their standard errors but rather the standard error of their difference." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 227]

The tuning takes the standard error (SE) of each habitat definition's difference from the best over watershed groups,
the units it leaves out, as the book does over sites [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 228]. Every habitat
definition within `r val("se_region")` SE of the best is a close call, and the published table gives the range of
close calls beside the choice, closer to what the book asks than a single winner [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking,
p. 225]. The width of one SE is a convention neither book sets, and choosing the close call nearest `link`'s current
habitat definition is a decision the scores do not make.

Choosing among thousands of habitat definitions also flatters the winner's score. *Bayesian Data Analysis* warns that
when scores like these are used to choose a model, "the predictive performance estimate of the selected model is biased due to the selection process" [@gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata, p. 182],
and names the remedy, a second level of left-out data. The tuning's check on the choosing (choosing on four folds and
scoring the choice on the fifth) was meant to be that, but the scores it chooses from came from fits that included
the fifth fold, so its test data were not fully left out. The check reports on the choosing only; it moves no choice
and no grade.

## What does the prior do? {#prior}

A regularising prior is sceptical: it slows how fast a model learns from the sample, and keeps an estimate finite
where the data alone would let it run away. Where one data set or period caught the species every time, or never,
nothing in the data stops its sampling term: the fit pushes it toward infinity, which is called separation. The tuning
gives the sampling terms a normal prior with a standard deviation of `r val("prior_sd")` on the scorer's complementary
log-log scale, the scale on which the scorer adds up its terms. On that scale a step of one multiplies the underlying
rate of catching by e, about 2.7, so a step of `r val("prior_sd")` multiplies it by about `r round(exp(prior_sd))`.

*Bayesian Data Analysis* uses the same scale, 2.5, for its default prior on logistic regression coefficients, but a
Cauchy prior, on every coefficient but the constant [@gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata, p. 416]. A Cauchy distribution is
bell-shaped like the normal, with far heavier tails: it pulls a modest estimate toward zero much as the normal does,
but leaves room for a truly large one. Beyond three times the scale from zero lies
`r sprintf("%.1f %%", 100 * p_norm)` of the normal and `r sprintf("%.0f %%", 100 * p_cauchy)` of the Cauchy. So the
tuning's normal holds a runaway sampling term harder than a Cauchy would; whether a Cauchy would move any score has not
been tested. The habitat definition itself carries no prior.

```{r prior, fig.cap = paste0("The two priors at scale 2.5: the normal the tuning uses (solid) and the Cauchy that *Bayesian Data Analysis* uses by default (dashed). The dotted lines mark three scales from zero; the top axis gives what a coefficient at each point multiplies the rate of catching by.")}
xs <- seq(-12, 12, by = 0.05)
pd <- rbind(data.frame(x = xs, density = stats::dnorm(xs, 0, prior_sd), prior = "normal, the tuning's"),
            data.frame(x = xs, density = stats::dcauchy(xs, 0, prior_sd), prior = "Cauchy, BDA3's default"))
brk <- c(-7.5, -2.5, 0, 2.5, 7.5)
ggplot(pd, aes(x, density, linetype = prior)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-7.5, 7.5), linetype = "dotted", colour = "#888888") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, colour = "#2c5f8a") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("normal, the tuning's" = "solid", "Cauchy, BDA3's default" = "dashed"), name = NULL,
                        breaks = c("normal, the tuning's", "Cauchy, BDA3's default")) +
  scale_x_continuous("coefficient, complementary log-log scale", breaks = brk,
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~., breaks = brk, name = "rate of catching multiplied by",
                                         labels = function(b) paste0("\u00d7", signif(exp(b), 2)))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The prior is fitted as a penalty, which finds the single most probable value and no more:

> "Ridge regression does not compute a posterior distribution." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 216]

So the tuning carries no uncertainty from the prior into its thresholds, which it reports as one choice and the range
of close calls, and no simulation of what the prior implies for the catch has been run
[@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 328]. The scorer also keeps a fallback, a fit without the prior, for a
fold whose usual fit would lose a term; by the way the prior is built the sampling terms cannot send a fold there, but
that rests on an argument, not a check.

## Are watershed groups pooled? {#pooling}

A model can give each watershed group its own base rate, learned from that group alone, or let the groups share what
they have in common, so a group with few sites borrows from the rest. The second, partial pooling, helps most where a
group has little data:

> "Smaller ponds produce more error, but the partial pooling estimates are better on average, especially in smaller ponds." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 413]

The scorer gives each watershed group its own base rate, which is cheap enough to score thousands of habitat
definitions and answers the within-group question above. A habitat definition earns its score inside a group by
separating the sites that caught the species from those that did not. A group where no site caught it, or every site
did, has nothing to separate: its own base rate explains every site, and runs to zero or to certainty, the separation
the prior stops for the sampling terms. Such a group says nothing about which habitat definition is better, so the
scorer drops it. Chinook rearing's sites fall in `r n0(ch$groups)` watershed groups; the scorer keeps the
`r n0(ch$groups_both)` with both catches and misses, and drops `r n0(ch$groups_none)` where no site caught chinook and
`r n0(ch$groups_all)` where every site did. In every species and stage the groups that caught nothing outnumber those
that caught everywhere, and for `r words_and(vapply(under_half, key_words, ""))` more than half the groups are
dropped.

```{r groups, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = "The watershed groups each species and stage's sites fall in: kept by the scorer because their sites hold both catches and misses, or dropped because no site caught the species or every site did. Spawning counts spawner evidence rather than a catch."}
gd <- rbind(data.frame(key = sc$key, kind = "kept: catches and misses", n = sc$groups_both),
            data.frame(key = sc$key, kind = "dropped: none caught", n = sc$groups_none),
            data.frame(key = sc$key, kind = "dropped: every site caught", n = sc$groups_all))
gd$label <- factor(vapply(gd$key, key_words, ""), levels = rev(vapply(sc$key[order(sc$groups)], key_words, "")))
gd$kind <- factor(gd$kind, levels = c("dropped: every site caught", "dropped: none caught", "kept: catches and misses"))
ggplot(gd, aes(n, label, fill = kind)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(data = gd[gd$n >= 4, ], aes(label = n), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 2.8,
            colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("kept: catches and misses" = "#2c5f8a", "dropped: none caught" = "#a9a9a9",
                               "dropped: every site caught" = "#d08c3c"), name = NULL,
                    breaks = c("kept: catches and misses", "dropped: none caught", "dropped: every site caught")) +
  labs(x = "watershed groups", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

These are the groups partial pooling would keep, letting a small group where nothing was caught borrow a base rate
from the rest instead of running to zero. The curve does pool the groups it is given: it learns a spread of base rates
across them. But it is fitted on at most the groups the scorer keeps, and each left-out group is still scored by its
own refitted base rate, so the pooled spread is never used to predict a group the curve has not seen. Grades are
still drawn for every stream the species can reach that has a size and a slope, in the dropped groups too.

The grade describes an average group, leaving each group's own base rate out [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking,
p. 428], which is the right reading for a map that compares streams across the province. But because every score
refits each group's base rate, no score has tested how well the grade compares a stream in one group with a stream in
another.

## Is the publishing test a fair comparison? {#publishing-test}

The publishing test compares the curve's deviance on the left-out folds with that of no habitat definition, on the
same sites and folds. This is the comparison the books teach, and it does not need to charge the curve again for its flexibility,
because the curve's smoothness is already penalised as it is fitted. But it is a point comparison with no standard
error, so any improvement publishes, and the curve's variables come from the choice made on the same folds. It
withholds `r words_and(vapply(withheld, key_words, ""))`. Its closest call, `r key_words(closest$key)`, was
`r if (closest$grade_withheld) "withheld" else "published"` by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(closest$margin))` in deviance.

```{r publishing, fig.height = 2.8, fig.cap = "The publishing test for each species and stage: the curve's deviance on the left-out folds less that of no habitat definition, with the value beside each point. Left of the dashed line at zero the curve predicts better and its grades are published; at zero or right of it they are withheld."}
pt <- curved
pt$diff <- -pt$margin
pt$label <- factor(vapply(pt$key, key_words, ""), levels = vapply(pt$key[order(pt$diff)], key_words, ""))
pt$grade <- ifelse(pt$grade_withheld, "withheld", "published")
ggplot(pt, aes(diff, label, colour = grade)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#555555") +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  geom_label(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", diff)), nudge_y = 0.36, size = 2.8, label.size = 0, fill = "white",
             label.padding = unit(0.1, "lines"), show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(published = "#2c5f8a", withheld = "#b5452b"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "curve's deviance less no habitat definition's", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The two sides of the publishing test also differ at one kind of site. Where a left-out site comes from a data set or period the
fit never saw, the no-habitat-definition side, which runs through the scorer, gives it the reference level, the
prior's centre; the curve gives it the most common level in the fit. So the two sides treat that site differently.

## What else differs? {#else}

- **Effort is fitted, not fixed.** The area fished enters with a fitted slope rather than as a fixed exposure (an
  offset), so the catch rate per square metre fished can rise or fall with the area fished: the hypothesis
  *Statistical Rethinking* describes for a free coefficient on the log of exposure
  [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 357]. Electrofishing a larger area plausibly catches less per square
  metre.
- **A miss is a miss at that visit.** The response is whether a crew caught the species on one visit, so a species
  present and missed reads as absent [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 499]. The grade says so: it is expected
  use per standard electrofishing visit, not habitat quality. Telling the two apart needs repeat visits.
- **The inputs are carried as exact.** A site's place on the stream, its slope and its modelled flow are each
  estimates. The tuning drops the worst-placed sites and reads the rest as measured, where the book carries such
  error into the model [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 495].

## Does a stream's slope depend on the catch? {#cuts}

A predictor should not be shaped by the outcome it predicts. The habitat definitions read the slope of the stretch of
stream, or segment, a site sits on, and `link` cuts a stream into segments at, among other places, the highest record
of each species it models on that stream. So a site that caught fish is more likely to start a short segment of its
own, whose slope is worked out from the stream just above the catch. `link`'s earlier build cut at every record; the
build the published tuning reads cuts only at the highest, among other changes, and there a site with fish starts its
own segment less often than before, but still several times as often as an empty site. Its minimal network makes no
cut at fish records, crossings or the ends of stretches whose habitat was mapped by hand; it still cuts where one
Atlas line meets the next, at natural barriers and at slopes a species cannot pass. There a site with fish starts its
own segment about as often as an empty one.

```{r cuts, fig.height = 2.8, fig.cap = "The share of site visits on the stream branch that start a segment of their own, for visits that caught fish and visits that did not, on link's full network as the earlier tuning read it, as the published tuning reads it, and on its minimal network."}
nets <- c(published_92 = "full network, earlier tuning", published_145 = "full network, published tuning",
          minimal = "minimal network")
pr$net <- factor(nets[pr$network], levels = rev(nets))
# none first, so the dodge draws the visits with fish above them
pr$catch <- factor(ifelse(pr$catch_status == "fish", "caught fish", "caught none"), levels = c("caught none", "caught fish"))
ggplot(pr, aes(at_site_pct, net, fill = catch)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = vapply(at_site_pct, pct, "")), position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), hjust = -0.15,
            size = 2.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("caught fish" = "#2c5f8a", "caught none" = "#a9a9a9"), name = NULL,
                    breaks = c("caught fish", "caught none")) +
  scale_x_continuous("visits starting a segment of their own (%)", limits = c(0, 100),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.04))) +
  labs(y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The network moves the result. Tuned on the minimal network, chinook rearing's steepest slope is `r lim_pct("minimal")`
rather than the published `r lim_pct("published")`, and it is `r lim_pct("parent")` again when each segment of the full
network reads the slope of the minimal segment it lies in, the form in which a habitat definition tuned on the minimal
network would be applied. The minimal network leaves out three kinds of cut at once, and its build is a slightly
earlier `link`, so these runs cannot say how much of the change comes from the cuts at fish records alone. The article
[Splitting streams at fish records shifts the steepest slope mapped as habitat](tuning-stream-splits.html) shows this in
full. Whether to tune on the minimal network is a decision not yet made.

## What do we test next? {#next}

- **Three fixes to the tuning** (`r issue(203)`): the curve gives a site from an unfamiliar data set or period the
  reference level, as the scorer does; a run stops if the scorer ever fits a fold without its prior, so that rests on
  a check; and the check on the choosing is either nested, each fold's choice made from fits that never saw it, or
  described as what it is.
- **A pooled curve, scored both ways** (`r issue(186)`), for chinook and westslope cutthroat trout rearing: a full
  posterior with priors on the smooths, and the groups with only catches or only misses kept. Today's curve and the
  pooled one are each scored both by every left-out group's own refitted base rate and as a new group drawn from the
  spread of groups, since a new-group score for one beside an own-base-rate score for the other compares nothing. Two
  cheap tests ride with it: the area fished as a fixed exposure, and a simulation of what the prior implies for the
  catch.
- **Tuning on the minimal network** (`r issue(120)`): every published species and stage has been tuned on it, and chinook
  rearing also through each full segment's minimal parent; none has been published, and whether to tune on it is
  still to decide.
- **Slopes measured other ways** (`r issue(70)`): modelled slopes checked against field-measured ones, and slopes over
  fixed lengths of stream scored beside `link`'s segment slope.

## What this review did not test {#limits}

- It reads the method and fits nothing; how much each change moves a score is measured by the work that makes it.
- Occupancy models, which separate a missed species from an absent one, are named in *Statistical Rethinking* but
  not taught there, and penalised splines are named in *Bayesian Data Analysis* without the smoothing library's
  penalty scale, so this review stops at what the books say.
- It describes the code at commit `r x$meta$commit` and the run whose summaries this article's data, written on
  `r x$meta$written`, read.

## Terms {#terms}

- **Base rate.** How often the species is caught in one watershed group, other things equal; the scorer fits one per
  group.
- **Cauchy distribution.** A bell-shaped distribution with far heavier tails than the normal; as a prior it pulls
  most estimates toward zero but leaves room for a large one.
- **Close calls.** Habitat definitions whose scores lie within one standard error of their difference from the best.
- **Complementary log-log scale.** The scale on which the scorer adds its terms; a step of one multiplies the
  underlying rate of catching by e, about 2.7.
- **Curve.** A smooth surface of how often the species is caught against stream size, distance to a river and slope,
  fitted after the choice; it gives each stream its grade.
- **Deviance.** How badly a model predicts the catch, summed over sites; lower is better.
- **Fold.** One of the `r val("folds")` sets the watershed groups are dealt into; each in turn is left out of the fit
  and scored.
- **Grade.** A stream's expected use per standard electrofishing visit, from the curve.
- **Habitat definition.** The few limits on a stream's size and slope that say where a species spawns or rears.
- **Minimal network.** `link`'s streams without the cuts at fish records, crossings and the ends of hand-mapped
  habitat; still cut where Atlas lines meet, at natural barriers and at slopes a species cannot pass.
- **Partial pooling.** Letting groups share what they have in common, so a group with little data borrows from the
  rest; the alternative is a base rate fitted to each group alone.
- **Penalty.** A prior fitted by finding its single most probable value (also called ridge regression), with no
  posterior.
- **Posterior.** The spread of values the data and the prior together allow.
- **Prior.** An assumption about a value made before seeing the data; a regularising prior keeps estimates modest.
- **Publishing test.** The check that publishes a species and stage's grades only if the curve scores better on the
  left-out folds than no habitat definition.
- **Sampling terms.** The data set a record comes from and its period: differences in how crews sampled that a habitat
  definition must not be credited for.
- **Score.** The scorer's deviance at sites in left-out watershed groups.
- **Scorer.** The regression of whether the species was caught on a habitat definition's sorting, with effort, the
  sampling terms and each group's base rate.
- **Separation.** Where a term or group meets only catches or only misses, so the fit pushes its value toward
  infinity.
- **Standard error of a difference.** How uncertain the gap between two scores is, worked out from the gap at each
  watershed group.
- **Watershed group.** One of the large drainages the Province divides its streams into.

## Software and citation {#software}

The tuning runs in the R package [`knowledge`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/knowledge/), on the habitat
definitions and streams of `link`. To cite this package:

```{r citation, results = "asis"}
cat(format(utils::citation("knowledge"), style = "text"), sep = "\n\n")
```
